lesson.title: Python for AI: Data Structures, NumPy Thinking and Clean Data Code
objectives: Explain why Python dominates AI engineering and where its performance limits are.
Choose the right built-in structure (list, tuple, dict, set) for a data task.
Describe vectorisation and broadcasting in NumPy and why they are faster than loops.
Distinguish views from copies and avoid common mutation bugs in data code.
Write a small, robust preprocessing step that handles missing values.
lesson.definition: Python for AI is the subset of Python skills an AI engineer uses every day: core data structures, functions and generators, and the scientific stack (NumPy, pandas) that stores numbers in contiguous typed arrays and runs operations in compiled code. The goal is code that is readable, correct with messy data and fast enough because heavy numeric work is pushed into vectorised libraries instead of Python loops.

theory.heading: Why Python is the language of AI
theory.body: Python itself is slow for tight numeric loops, but it is an excellent glue language. NumPy, PyTorch, TensorFlow and scikit-learn implement their heavy maths in C, C++ or CUDA and expose a Python API. An AI engineer writes the orchestration in Python and lets the libraries do the arithmetic. This is why interviewers care less about clever loops and more about whether you know how to keep work inside the fast libraries.
points: Huge ecosystem: NumPy, pandas, scikit-learn, PyTorch, Hugging Face, FastAPI.
Readable syntax makes experiments and reviews quick.
Performance comes from compiled back ends, not from the interpreter.

theory.heading: Built-in data structures and when to use each
theory.body: Lists are ordered and mutable, good for building sequences. Tuples are immutable, so they can be dictionary keys and signal fixed records such as (height, width). Dictionaries give average O(1) lookup by key and are ideal for vocabularies (token to id) and configuration. Sets give O(1) membership tests and remove duplicates, for example checking whether a word is a stop word.
points: list: ordered, mutable, O(1) append, O(n) membership test.
tuple: immutable, hashable when its items are hashable.
dict: key to value mapping, insertion ordered since Python 3.7.
set: unique items, fast membership and set algebra.

theory.heading: Vectorisation and broadcasting
theory.body: A NumPy array stores values of one dtype in a contiguous block of memory. An expression such as (X - X.mean(axis=0)) / X.std(axis=0) runs one optimised C loop over the whole array instead of millions of Python-level operations, which is often 10 to 100 times faster. Broadcasting lets arrays of different shapes combine: a (1000, 3) matrix minus a (3,) vector subtracts the vector from every row without copying it 1000 times. Shapes are compared from the right; each pair of dimensions must be equal or one of them must be 1.
points: Prefer array expressions over Python for loops for numeric work.
Know your shapes: most bugs in ML code are shape bugs.
axis=0 reduces over rows (one result per column); axis=1 reduces over columns.

theory.heading: Views, copies and mutation pitfalls
theory.body: Basic NumPy slicing returns a view that shares memory with the original, so writing to the slice changes the source array. Fancy indexing (with a list or boolean mask) returns a copy. In plain Python, assigning a list to a new name does not copy it, and a mutable default argument such as def f(x=[]) is shared across calls. These bugs silently corrupt training data, so call .copy() when you need independence.
points: arr[1:3] is a view; arr[[1, 2]] and arr[arr > 0] are copies.
Never use a mutable object as a default argument; use None and create it inside.
pandas may warn about chained assignment; use .loc for clear, single-step writes.

theory.heading: Handling large data and missing values
theory.body: Real datasets do not fit in memory and contain gaps. Generators (yield) stream records one at a time, so a 50 GB log file can be processed with constant memory. Missing values must be handled deliberately: drop them, impute them (mean, median, a constant) or add an indicator column. Imputation statistics must be computed on training data only and reused on validation and test data, otherwise information leaks from the evaluation set.
points: Use generators or chunked reads (pandas read_csv with chunksize) for big files.
NaN propagates through arithmetic; np.nanmean ignores it.
Fit preprocessing on the training split, then apply it everywhere.

example.title: Standardising features with broadcasting
example.body: Standardisation rescales each feature to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 so that features measured in different units (age in years, income in rupees) contribute comparably to distance-based or gradient-based models. With NumPy the whole matrix is standardised in one line, and the statistics are computed on the training split only.

code.source:
import numpy as np

X_train = np.array([[25, 30000.0], [32, 52000.0], [47, 91000.0]])
X_test = np.array([[29, 40000.0]])

mu = X_train.mean(axis=0)          # shape (2,)
sigma = X_train.std(axis=0)        # shape (2,)
sigma[sigma == 0] = 1.0            # avoid division by zero

X_train_s = (X_train - mu) / sigma  # (3, 2) - (2,) broadcasts per row
X_test_s = (X_test - mu) / sigma    # reuse training statistics
print(X_train_s.round(2))
print(X_test_s.round(2))

demonstration.description: Compare a Python loop with a vectorised NumPy expression on one million numbers. Both compute the same sum of squares, but the vectorised version runs in compiled code. Exact timings depend on the machine; the ratio is what matters.

code.source:
import time
import numpy as np

x = np.random.default_rng(0).random(1_000_000)

t = time.perf_counter()
total = 0.0
for v in x:
    total += v * v
loop_s = time.perf_counter() - t

t = time.perf_counter()
total_np = float(np.dot(x, x))
vec_s = time.perf_counter() - t

print(round(total, 3) == round(total_np, 3))
print(f'loop {loop_s:.3f}s, vectorised {vec_s:.4f}s')

demonstration.output:
True
loop 0.250s, vectorised 0.0007s   (typical laptop: the vectorised call is hundreds of times faster)

takeaways: Python is the glue; NumPy, PyTorch and similar libraries do the heavy maths in compiled code.
Pick data structures by access pattern: dict and set for fast lookup, list for order, tuple for fixed records.
Vectorise numeric work and learn broadcasting rules; check shapes constantly.
Slices are views and fancy indexing makes copies; copy explicitly when you need independence.
Stream large data with generators and compute preprocessing statistics on training data only.
Handle missing values deliberately and document the choice.

interview.question: What is the difference between a list and a NumPy array?
interview.answer: A list holds references to arbitrary Python objects of any type, so each element is boxed and operations run in the interpreter. A NumPy array holds one fixed dtype in contiguous memory, supports element-wise maths and broadcasting, and runs operations in optimised C, which makes it far faster and more memory-efficient for numbers.
interview.explanation: Strong answers mention contiguous memory, a single dtype and vectorised execution, then give a quick example such as adding two arrays without a loop.

interview.question: What is broadcasting? Give an example.
interview.answer: Broadcasting is NumPy's rule for combining arrays of different shapes without copying data. Shapes are aligned from the right and each dimension must match or be 1. For example, a (100, 3) matrix minus a (3,) vector of column means subtracts the means from every row.
interview.explanation: Mention the alignment rule and a realistic ML use such as feature centring or adding a bias vector to a batch of activations.

interview.question: Why should you avoid a mutable default argument such as def add(item, bucket=[])?
interview.answer: Default values are evaluated once when the function is defined, so every call that omits bucket shares and mutates the same list. Use bucket=None and create a new list inside the function.
interview.explanation: This is a classic Python screening question; explaining when defaults are evaluated shows real understanding.

interview.question: How would you process a 40 GB CSV file on a machine with 16 GB of RAM?
interview.answer: Stream it: read in chunks (pandas read_csv with chunksize, or a generator over lines), aggregate or transform each chunk and write results incrementally. Alternatives include columnar formats such as Parquet with only the needed columns, or engines such as Polars, DuckDB or Spark.
interview.explanation: Interviewers look for constant-memory thinking, choosing only needed columns and knowing when to switch to an out-of-core tool.

interview.question: Does the GIL stop Python from being useful for parallel ML workloads?
interview.answer: The Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time, which limits CPU-bound pure-Python threads. NumPy and PyTorch release the GIL inside compiled kernels, I/O-bound work benefits from threads or asyncio, and CPU-bound Python work can use multiprocessing (as PyTorch DataLoader workers do).
interview.explanation: A strong answer separates CPU-bound from I/O-bound work and notes that heavy maths already runs outside the GIL. Mentioning that free-threaded Python builds now exist is a bonus.

practice.title: Impute and standardise a feature column
practice.objective: Practise the everyday preprocessing step of handling missing values and computing z-scores, the operation StandardScaler performs.
practice.statement: Read one line of comma-separated values for a single numeric feature. Some values are the text NA (missing). Compute the mean and the population standard deviation of the present values only. Replace each NA with that mean, then convert every value to a z-score: (value - mean) / std. If std is 0, every z-score is 0. If no values are present, print only the line no data.
practice.input_format: One line of comma-separated tokens; each token is a number or NA (spaces around tokens may appear).
practice.output_format:
Four lines:
count=<present> missing=<missing>
mean=<mean with 2 decimals>
std=<std with 2 decimals>
the z-scores with 2 decimals separated by single spaces (print 0.00, never -0.00).
Or the single line no data.
constraints: NA is matched case-insensitively after trimming spaces.
Use the population standard deviation (divide by the number of present values).
practice.starter:
tokens = [t.strip() for t in input().split(',')]

# TODO: separate present values from NA, compute mean and std,
# impute, then print the four required lines
practice.solution:
import math

tokens = [t.strip() for t in input().split(',')]
values = [None if t.upper() == 'NA' else float(t) for t in tokens]
present = [v for v in values if v is not None]

def fmt(v):
    s = f'{v:.2f}'
    return '0.00' if s == '-0.00' else s

if not present:
    print('no data')
else:
    mean = sum(present) / len(present)
    std = math.sqrt(sum((v - mean) ** 2 for v in present) / len(present))
    filled = [mean if v is None else v for v in values]
    z = [(v - mean) / std if std > 0 else 0.0 for v in filled]
    print(f'count={len(present)} missing={len(values) - len(present)}')
    print(f'mean={fmt(mean)}')
    print(f'std={fmt(std)}')
    print(' '.join(fmt(v) for v in z))
explanation: Split on commas, trim each token and map NA to None and everything else to float.
Compute the mean and population standard deviation from present values only, so missing entries do not distort the statistics.
Impute each missing value with the mean, which gives it a z-score of exactly 0.
Guard the division: a constant column has std 0, so all z-scores are 0.
Format with two decimals and normalise -0.00 to 0.00 for clean output.

lesson.title: Linear Algebra Essentials: Vectors, Matrices and the Dot Product
objectives: Represent data, model weights and embeddings as vectors and matrices.
Compute and interpret dot products, norms and cosine similarity.
Apply the shape rule for matrix multiplication and spot shape errors quickly.
Explain transpose, identity, inverse, rank and eigenvectors at an interview level.
Implement matrix multiplication by hand with a shape check.
lesson.definition: Linear algebra is the mathematics of vectors (ordered lists of numbers) and matrices (rectangular grids of numbers) and the linear operations on them. In AI, a data point is a vector of features, a dataset is a matrix, a neural-network layer is a matrix multiplication followed by a non-linearity, and an embedding is a vector whose direction encodes meaning.

theory.heading: Why AI engineers need linear algebra
theory.body: Almost every model computes something of the form y = Wx + b. A batch of 64 images flattened to 784 pixels is a (64, 784) matrix; a dense layer with 128 units is a (784, 128) weight matrix; the forward pass is a single matrix product producing (64, 128). GPUs exist largely to do these products fast. Understanding shapes lets you read model code, debug errors such as 'mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied' and estimate compute cost.
points: Scalar: a single number. Vector: shape (n,). Matrix: shape (m, n). Tensor: any number of dimensions.
Datasets are matrices with rows as samples and columns as features.
Layer weights, attention scores and embeddings are all matrices.

theory.heading: Dot product, norms and cosine similarity
theory.body: The dot product a · b = sum of a_i * b_i measures how much two vectors point in the same direction, scaled by their lengths. The L2 norm ||a|| = sqrt(a · a) is a vector's length; the L1 norm is the sum of absolute values. Cosine similarity divides the dot product by both norms, giving a value from -1 to 1 that ignores length and compares only direction. This is exactly how semantic search compares text embeddings.
points: a · b = ||a|| ||b|| cos(theta).
Orthogonal vectors have dot product 0: they share no direction.
L2 norms appear in regularisation (weight decay) and in normalising embeddings.

theory.heading: Matrix multiplication and the shape rule
theory.body: For A with shape (m, n) and B with shape (n, p), the product AB has shape (m, p) and each entry is the dot product of a row of A with a column of B. The inner dimensions must match. Matrix multiplication is associative but not commutative: AB is usually not equal to BA, and BA may not even be defined. Multiplying an (m, n) by an (n, p) matrix costs about m * n * p multiply-adds, which is how you estimate FLOPs for a layer.
points: Inner dimensions must match; outer dimensions give the result shape.
Element-wise (Hadamard) product A * B is different from matrix product A @ B.
Transpose swaps rows and columns: (AB)^T = B^T A^T.

theory.heading: Special matrices, rank and inverse
theory.body: The identity matrix I leaves vectors unchanged. A square matrix is invertible when its columns are linearly independent, meaning its rank equals its size; otherwise information is lost and no inverse exists. The rank is the number of independent directions a matrix can produce. Low rank is central to modern AI: LoRA fine-tuning represents a weight update as the product of two thin matrices, which has low rank and far fewer parameters.
points: Rank = number of linearly independent rows or columns.
In practice we solve linear systems with stable solvers rather than computing inverses.
Low-rank factorisation compresses matrices (SVD, LoRA).

theory.heading: Eigenvectors, SVD and where they appear
theory.body: An eigenvector v of a square matrix A satisfies Av = lambda v: A only stretches it by the eigenvalue lambda without changing its direction. Principal Component Analysis finds the eigenvectors of the data covariance matrix, which are the directions of greatest variance. Singular Value Decomposition (A = U Sigma V^T) generalises this to any matrix and underlies PCA, recommender systems and low-rank approximation.
points: PCA: project data onto the top eigenvectors to reduce dimensions.
SVD exists for every matrix, square or not.
Large singular values carry most of the information in a matrix.

example.title: A dense layer is one matrix product
example.body: A batch of 4 samples with 3 features passes through a layer with 2 output units. The weight matrix has shape (3, 2) and the bias has shape (2,). The output shape (4, 2) follows from the shape rule, and the bias is broadcast to every row.

code.source:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
B = np.array([[7, 8], [9, 10], [11, 12]])
print(A @ B)
print((B @ A).shape)
print(np.linalg.matrix_rank(np.array([[1, 2], [2, 4]])))

takeaways: Data, weights and embeddings are vectors and matrices; check shapes first when debugging.
(m, n) @ (n, p) gives (m, p); inner dimensions must match.
Dot product measures alignment; cosine similarity compares direction only.
Matrix multiplication is not commutative and is different from element-wise multiplication.
Rank counts independent directions; low-rank ideas power PCA, SVD and LoRA.
A layer's compute cost is roughly m * n * p multiply-adds.

interview.question: What is a dot product and what does it tell you?
interview.answer: It is the sum of element-wise products of two equal-length vectors. Its sign and size show how aligned the vectors are: positive when they point the same way, zero when orthogonal, negative when opposite, scaled by their lengths.
interview.explanation: Link it to ML: neurons compute dot products of inputs and weights, and attention scores are dot products of queries and keys.

interview.question: Why is cosine similarity preferred over raw dot product for comparing text embeddings?
interview.answer: Cosine similarity normalises by vector length, so it compares meaning (direction) rather than magnitude, which can depend on text length or model quirks. If embeddings are already L2-normalised, dot product and cosine give the same ranking.
interview.explanation: Mentioning the normalised-embedding shortcut shows you understand how vector databases are configured in practice.

interview.question: A layer has input (32, 512) and weights (512, 256). What is the output shape and roughly how many multiply-adds are needed?
interview.answer: The output is (32, 256). The cost is about 32 * 512 * 256 = 4,194,304 multiply-adds.
interview.explanation: Interviewers check that you can apply the shape rule and estimate compute, a skill used when sizing models and hardware.

interview.question: What is the rank of a matrix and why does low rank matter in AI?
interview.answer: Rank is the number of linearly independent rows or columns. A low-rank matrix can be written as the product of two thin matrices, so it can be stored and learned with far fewer parameters. LoRA uses this to fine-tune large models cheaply, and PCA uses it to compress data.
interview.explanation: Connecting an abstract concept to a modern technique such as LoRA is what distinguishes a strong answer.

interview.question: What are eigenvectors and how does PCA use them?
interview.answer: An eigenvector of a square matrix keeps its direction when multiplied by the matrix; it is only scaled by its eigenvalue. PCA computes eigenvectors of the covariance matrix (or uses SVD of centred data); the eigenvectors with the largest eigenvalues are the directions of greatest variance and become the principal components.
interview.explanation: A strong answer notes that data must be centred first and that the explained variance ratio is used to choose how many components to keep.

practice.title: Matrix multiplication with a shape check
practice.objective: Implement the core operation behind every neural-network layer and practise the shape rule.
practice.statement: Read matrix A (m x n) and matrix B (n2 x p) of integers. If n is not equal to n2, print shape mismatch: (m,n) @ (n2,p). Otherwise compute C = A @ B, print its shape, its rows, and its trace (sum of the main diagonal) if C is square, or trace=n/a if it is not.
practice.input_format:
Line 1: m n. Next m lines: n integers each (rows of A).
Next line: n2 p. Next n2 lines: p integers each (rows of B).
practice.output_format:
Either the single line shape mismatch: (m,n) @ (n2,p) or: shape x

, then m lines with the row values separated by spaces, then trace= or trace=n/a.
constraints: Do not use any library; use nested loops or comprehensions.
practice.starter:
import sys

data = sys.stdin.read().split()
# TODO: parse A and B, check shapes, multiply, print shape, rows and trace
practice.solution:
import sys

data = sys.stdin.read().split()
pos = 0

def read_matrix():
    global pos
    r, c = int(data[pos]), int(data[pos + 1])
    pos += 2
    rows = []
    for _ in range(r):
        rows.append([int(v) for v in data[pos:pos + c]])
        pos += c
    return r, c, rows

m, n, A = read_matrix()
n2, p, B = read_matrix()
if n != n2:
    print(f'shape mismatch: ({m},{n}) @ ({n2},{p})')
else:
    C = [[sum(A[i][k] * B[k][j] for k in range(n)) for j in range(p)] for i in range(m)]
    print(f'shape {m} x {p}')
    for row in C:
        print(' '.join(str(v) for v in row))
    if m == p:
        print(f'trace={sum(C[i][i] for i in range(m))}')
    else:
        print('trace=n/a')
explanation: Read all tokens at once and parse each matrix by its declared shape.
Check the inner dimensions first; this is the same rule PyTorch enforces.
Each C[i][j] is the dot product of row i of A and column j of B.
The result has the outer dimensions (m, p); compute the trace only when m equals p.

quiz.question: A is (8, 5) and B is (5, 3). What is the shape of A @ B?
quiz.explanation: Inner dimensions (5 and 5) match, and the result takes the outer dimensions (8, 3).

b = [4, -2, 0]
print(sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b)))
quiz.explanation: 1*4 + 2*(-2) + 3*0 = 4 - 4 + 0 = 0, so the vectors are orthogonal.

options: They point in nearly opposite directions
One of them has zero length
quiz.explanation: Cosine similarity ranges from -1 to 1; values near -1 mean opposite directions.

options: Make the layer's input size 784 so its weight is (784, 10)
quiz.explanation: The inner dimensions 784 and 512 do not match; the layer expects 512 features but receives 784, so its input size must be 784.

quiz.question: Which technique relies most directly on low-rank matrix factorisation to reduce trainable parameters?
quiz.explanation: LoRA represents a weight update as the product of two thin matrices, a low-rank factorisation with far fewer parameters.

lesson.title: Probability and Statistics for Machine Learning
objectives: Explain random variables, distributions, expectation and variance in plain terms.
Apply conditional probability and Bayes' theorem to realistic problems.
Recognise the normal, Bernoulli, binomial and categorical distributions in ML.
Connect maximum likelihood to common loss functions such as MSE and cross-entropy.
Avoid base-rate mistakes when interpreting classifier outputs.
lesson.definition: Probability is the mathematics of uncertainty: it assigns numbers between 0 and 1 to events and describes how likely different outcomes are. Statistics uses data to estimate those probabilities and the parameters of distributions. Machine learning models are statistical models: a classifier outputs a probability distribution over classes and training chooses the parameters that make the observed data most likely.

theory.heading: Random variables and distributions
theory.body: A random variable maps an uncertain outcome to a number, such as whether a transaction is fraud (0 or 1) or tomorrow's temperature. Its distribution says how probable each value is. Discrete variables have a probability mass function; continuous variables have a probability density. ML uses a small set of distributions repeatedly, and knowing them explains model design choices.
points: Bernoulli: one yes/no trial, used for binary classification outputs.
Categorical: one of K classes, the output of a softmax layer.
Binomial: number of successes in n trials, e.g. clicks out of impressions.
Normal (Gaussian): bell curve, used for noise, weight initialisation and many natural measurements.

theory.heading: Expectation, variance and descriptive statistics
theory.body: The expectation (mean) is the probability-weighted average of a variable. Variance measures spread as the expected squared distance from the mean, and standard deviation is its square root in the original units. The median is robust to outliers, which is why it is often better for skewed data such as salaries or response latencies. Sample statistics estimate population ones and have their own uncertainty, which is why A/B tests report confidence intervals.
points: E[aX + b] = aE[X] + b; Var(aX + b) = a^2 Var(X).
Use median and percentiles (p95, p99) for skewed data like latency.
Covariance and correlation measure how two variables move together; correlation is not causation.

theory.heading: Conditional probability and Bayes' theorem
theory.body: P(A | B) is the probability of A given that B happened. Bayes' theorem reverses a conditional: P(A | B) = P(B | A) P(A) / P(B). The prior P(A) is what we believed before the evidence, the likelihood P(B | A) is how compatible the evidence is with A, and the posterior P(A | B) is the updated belief. Ignoring the prior is the base-rate fallacy: a 99 percent sensitive test for a rare disease still produces mostly false positives.
points: P(B) = P(B | A)P(A) + P(B | not A)P(not A) (law of total probability).
Naive Bayes classifiers apply Bayes' theorem with an independence assumption between features.

theory.heading: Maximum likelihood and loss functions
theory.body: Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) chooses parameters that make the observed data most probable. Taking the negative log turns products into sums and maximisation into minimisation, which gives the losses we train with. Assuming Gaussian noise around predictions gives mean squared error; assuming Bernoulli or categorical labels gives binary or categorical cross-entropy. Adding a prior on the weights (MAP estimation) gives regularisation such as L2.

Cross-entropy (log loss) corresponds to Bernoulli or categorical likelihood.
A Gaussian prior on weights corresponds to L2 regularisation.

theory.heading: Sampling, the central limit theorem and hypothesis tests
theory.body: The central limit theorem says that the mean of many independent samples is approximately normally distributed, whatever the original distribution. This justifies confidence intervals and significance tests used to compare models or run A/B tests. A p-value is the probability of seeing results at least as extreme as observed if there were really no difference; it is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
points: Larger samples shrink the standard error by a factor of sqrt(n).
Run enough samples before concluding a new model is better.
Multiple comparisons inflate false discoveries.

example.title: Why a 99 percent accurate fraud alert is mostly wrong
example.body: Suppose 1 percent of transactions are fraud, the detector catches 99 percent of fraud (sensitivity) and correctly clears 95 percent of genuine transactions (specificity). Bayes' theorem shows that only about 17 percent of flagged transactions are actually fraud, because the 5 percent false-alarm rate is applied to the 99 percent of genuine traffic.

lesson.title: The Machine Learning Workflow: From Problem Framing to Baselines
objectives: Describe the end-to-end ML lifecycle from problem framing to monitoring.
Frame a business problem as an ML task with a measurable target and metric.
Split data into train, validation and test sets correctly, including time-based splits.
Identify and prevent data leakage.
Build a simple baseline before training complex models.
lesson.definition: The machine learning workflow is the repeatable sequence of steps used to turn a business problem into a working model: frame the problem, collect and understand data, prepare features, split the data, establish a baseline, train and tune models, evaluate on held-out data, deploy and monitor. Each step has typical failure modes, and most real-world ML failures come from data and process mistakes rather than from the choice of algorithm.

theory.heading: Problem framing comes first
theory.body: Before touching data, define what decision the model will support, what the prediction target is, how success is measured and what happens when the model is wrong. 'Reduce churn' becomes 'predict whether a subscriber cancels within 30 days, ranked by risk, so the retention team can call the top 500 each week'. This framing decides the label, the prediction time, the metric (for example precision in the top 500) and whether ML is even needed. Sometimes a rule or a SQL query is enough.
points: Define the target, the prediction moment and the action taken on the prediction.
Pick a business metric and an offline ML metric that correlates with it.
Ask whether a simple rule would solve the problem first.

theory.heading: The lifecycle step by step
theory.body: A typical project loops through these stages many times. Exploratory data analysis reveals missing values, skew, label noise and imbalance. Feature engineering turns raw data into model inputs. Training and hyperparameter tuning happen on training and validation data. A final, untouched test set gives an unbiased estimate before deployment. After deployment, monitoring watches for data drift and performance decay, which triggers retraining.
points: Collect and explore data (EDA).
Clean, engineer and encode features.
Split data; train, tune and compare against a baseline.
Evaluate once on the test set; deploy behind an API or batch job.
Monitor, collect feedback and retrain.

theory.heading: Train, validation and test splits
theory.body: The training set fits model parameters, the validation set chooses hyperparameters and models, and the test set is used once to report final performance. Reusing the test set for decisions slowly overfits to it. When samples are independent, random or stratified splits work; stratification keeps class proportions similar in each split. When data is ordered in time, such as transactions or demand, split by time: train on the past and test on the future, because that is how the model will be used.
points: Common ratios: 70/15/15 or 80/10/10, adjusted for dataset size.
Use k-fold cross-validation when data is small.
Group-aware splits keep all rows from one user or patient in the same split.

theory.heading: Data leakage
theory.body: Leakage happens when information that would not be available at prediction time reaches the model during training. Classic examples are fitting a scaler on the full dataset before splitting, including a feature that is recorded after the outcome (such as 'refund issued' when predicting complaints), random splits on time-series data and duplicate rows across train and test. Leakage produces excellent offline scores and disappointing production performance.
points: Fit all preprocessing inside the training fold only (scikit-learn Pipelines help).
Check every feature's timestamp against the prediction moment.
Deduplicate before splitting.

theory.heading: Baselines and iteration
theory.body: A baseline is the simplest reasonable predictor: the majority class for classification, the mean or last value for regression, or a simple heuristic. It sets the bar a model must clear and catches bugs: if a deep network barely beats predicting the majority class, either the problem is hard or something is wrong. Then iterate with simple models (logistic regression, gradient-boosted trees) before reaching for complex ones.
points: Majority-class accuracy reveals class imbalance immediately.
Gradient-boosted trees are a strong default for tabular data.
Change one thing at a time and track every experiment.

example.title: A leak-free scikit-learn workflow
example.body: A Pipeline bundles preprocessing and the model so that cross-validation fits the scaler only on each training fold. A DummyClassifier provides the majority-class baseline to compare against.

from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=0)

baseline = DummyClassifier(strategy='most_frequent').fit(X_tr, y_tr)
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
print('cv:', cross_val_score(model, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean().round(3))
model.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print('baseline test:', round(baseline.score(X_te, y_te), 3))
print('model test:', round(model.score(X_te, y_te), 3))

interview.question: Walk me through the steps of an ML project.
interview.answer: Frame the problem and metric, collect and explore data, clean and engineer features, split into train, validation and test, build a baseline, train and tune models, evaluate on the test set, deploy, then monitor and retrain.
interview.explanation: Interviewers want structure plus judgement: mention that most time goes into data and that monitoring closes the loop.

interview.question: Why do we need both a validation set and a test set?
interview.answer: The validation set is used repeatedly to choose hyperparameters and models, so its score becomes optimistically biased. The test set is held back and used once to give an unbiased estimate of performance on new data.
interview.explanation: Mention cross-validation as an alternative to a fixed validation set when data is limited.

interview.question: What is data leakage? Give two examples.
interview.answer: Leakage is when training uses information unavailable at prediction time. Examples: scaling or imputing with statistics from the full dataset before splitting, and using a feature recorded after the outcome, such as 'account closed date' when predicting churn.
interview.explanation: Strong answers also say how to prevent it: pipelines, time-aware splits, feature timestamp audits and deduplication.

interview.question: How would you split data for a model that predicts next week's sales?
interview.answer: Use a time-based split: train on older periods and validate and test on later periods, ideally with rolling or expanding windows (walk-forward validation). A random split would let the model see the future.
interview.explanation: This tests whether you think about how the model is used in production, not just about the mechanics of splitting.

interview.question: Your new model reaches 95 percent accuracy. Why might that not be impressive?
interview.answer: If 95 percent of samples belong to one class, predicting that class always also gives 95 percent. Compare against a majority-class baseline and use metrics suited to imbalance such as precision, recall, F1 or PR-AUC.
interview.explanation: This shows baseline thinking and leads naturally into evaluation metrics (Day 8).

practice.title: Time-based split with a majority-class baseline
practice.objective: Practise a leak-free split for time-ordered data and compute the baseline every model must beat.
practice.statement: Labels are given in time order. Hold out the last n_test labels as the test set, where n_test = floor(n * fraction), clamped to the range 1 to n - 1. Using the training labels only, find the majority class (break ties by choosing the alphabetically smallest label). Print the split sizes, the training label counts, the baseline label and the baseline's accuracy on the test set.

Line 1: the test fraction (a decimal between 0 and 1).
Line 2: n labels separated by spaces, oldest first (n >= 2).

train_counts=<label:count pairs sorted by label, separated by spaces>

0.25
no no yes no yes no no yes

constraints: Labels are non-empty strings without spaces.
Compute floor(n * fraction) with a small tolerance, e.g. int(n * fraction + 1e-9).

labels = input().split()

practice.solution:
from collections import Counter

frac = float(input())
labels = input().split()
n = len(labels)
n_test = int(n * frac + 1e-9)
n_test = max(1, min(n - 1, n_test))
train, test = labels[:n - n_test], labels[n - n_test:]

counts = Counter(train)
baseline = sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))[0][0]
accuracy = sum(1 for y in test if y == baseline) / len(test)

print(f'train={len(train)} test={len(test)}')
print('train_counts=' + ' '.join(f'{k}:{counts[k]}' for k in sorted(counts)))
print(f'baseline={baseline}')
print(f'test_accuracy={accuracy:.2f}')
explanation: Compute the test size from the fraction and clamp it so both splits are non-empty.
Take the most recent labels as the test set; never shuffle time-ordered data.
Count labels on the training split only, so the baseline does not peek at the test set.
Sort by descending count, then by label, to break ties deterministically.
Accuracy is the share of test labels equal to the baseline prediction.

questions.topic: Python for AI: Data Structures, NumPy Thinking and Clean Data Code
questions.question: What is the difference between a list and a NumPy array?
questions.answer: A list holds references to arbitrary Python objects of any type, so each element is boxed and operations run in the interpreter. A NumPy array holds one fixed dtype in contiguous memory, supports element-wise maths and broadcasting, and runs operations in optimised C, which makes it far faster and more memory-efficient for numbers.
questions.explanation: Strong answers mention contiguous memory, a single dtype and vectorised execution, then give a quick example such as adding two arrays without a loop.

questions.topic: Python for AI: Data Structures, NumPy Thinking and Clean Data Code
questions.question: What is broadcasting? Give an example.
questions.answer: Broadcasting is NumPy's rule for combining arrays of different shapes without copying data. Shapes are aligned from the right and each dimension must match or be 1. For example, a (100, 3) matrix minus a (3,) vector of column means subtracts the means from every row.
questions.explanation: Mention the alignment rule and a realistic ML use such as feature centring or adding a bias vector to a batch of activations.

questions.topic: Python for AI: Data Structures, NumPy Thinking and Clean Data Code
questions.question: Why should you avoid a mutable default argument such as def add(item, bucket=[])?
questions.answer: Default values are evaluated once when the function is defined, so every call that omits bucket shares and mutates the same list. Use bucket=None and create a new list inside the function.
questions.explanation: This is a classic Python screening question; explaining when defaults are evaluated shows real understanding.

questions.question: How would you process a 40 GB CSV file on a machine with 16 GB of RAM?
questions.answer: Stream it: read in chunks (pandas read_csv with chunksize, or a generator over lines), aggregate or transform each chunk and write results incrementally. Alternatives include columnar formats such as Parquet with only the needed columns, or engines such as Polars, DuckDB or Spark.
questions.explanation: Interviewers look for constant-memory thinking, choosing only needed columns and knowing when to switch to an out-of-core tool.

questions.question: Does the GIL stop Python from being useful for parallel ML workloads?
questions.answer: The Global Interpreter Lock lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time, which limits CPU-bound pure-Python threads. NumPy and PyTorch release the GIL inside compiled kernels, I/O-bound work benefits from threads or asyncio, and CPU-bound Python work can use multiprocessing (as PyTorch DataLoader workers do).
questions.explanation: A strong answer separates CPU-bound from I/O-bound work and notes that heavy maths already runs outside the GIL. Mentioning that free-threaded Python builds now exist is a bonus.

questions.question: What is a dot product and what does it tell you?
questions.answer: It is the sum of element-wise products of two equal-length vectors. Its sign and size show how aligned the vectors are: positive when they point the same way, zero when orthogonal, negative when opposite, scaled by their lengths.
questions.explanation: Link it to ML: neurons compute dot products of inputs and weights, and attention scores are dot products of queries and keys.

questions.explanation: Mentioning the normalised-embedding shortcut shows you understand how vector databases are configured in practice.

questions.answer: Frame the problem and metric, collect and explore data, clean and engineer features, split into train, validation and test, build a baseline, train and tune models, evaluate on the test set, deploy, then monitor and retrain.
questions.explanation: Interviewers want structure plus judgement: mention that most time goes into data and that monitoring closes the loop.

questions.topic: The Machine Learning Workflow: From Problem Framing to Baselines
questions.question: Why do we need both a validation set and a test set?
questions.answer: The validation set is used repeatedly to choose hyperparameters and models, so its score becomes optimistically biased. The test set is held back and used once to give an unbiased estimate of performance on new data.
questions.explanation: Mention cross-validation as an alternative to a fixed validation set when data is limited.

questions.topic: The Machine Learning Workflow: From Problem Framing to Baselines
questions.question: What is data leakage? Give two examples.
questions.answer: Leakage is when training uses information unavailable at prediction time. Examples: scaling or imputing with statistics from the full dataset before splitting, and using a feature recorded after the outcome, such as 'account closed date' when predicting churn.
questions.explanation: Strong answers also say how to prevent it: pipelines, time-aware splits, feature timestamp audits and deduplication.

questions.topic: The Machine Learning Workflow: From Problem Framing to Baselines
questions.question: How would you split data for a model that predicts next week's sales?
questions.answer: Use a time-based split: train on older periods and validate and test on later periods, ideally with rolling or expanding windows (walk-forward validation). A random split would let the model see the future.
questions.explanation: This tests whether you think about how the model is used in production, not just about the mechanics of splitting.

questions.topic: The Machine Learning Workflow: From Problem Framing to Baselines
questions.question: Your new model reaches 95 percent accuracy. Why might that not be impressive?
questions.answer: If 95 percent of samples belong to one class, predicting that class always also gives 95 percent. Compare against a majority-class baseline and use metrics suited to imbalance such as precision, recall, F1 or PR-AUC.
questions.explanation: This shows baseline thinking and leads naturally into evaluation metrics (Day 8).

days.title: Python for AI: Data Structures, NumPy Thinking and Clean Data Code
days.focus: Python for AI is the subset of Python skills an AI engineer uses every day: core data structures, functions and generators, and the scientific stack (NumPy, pandas) that stores numbers in contiguous typed arrays and runs operations in compiled code. The goal is code that is readable, correct with messy data and fast enough because heavy numeric work is pushed into vectorised libraries instead of Python loops.
objectives: Explain why Python dominates AI engineering and where its performance limits are.
Choose the right built-in structure (list, tuple, dict, set) for a data task.
Describe vectorisation and broadcasting in NumPy and why they are faster than loops.
Distinguish views from copies and avoid common mutation bugs in data code.
Write a small, robust preprocessing step that handles missing values.
days.assignment: Read one line of comma-separated values for a single numeric feature. Some values are the text NA (missing). Compute the mean and the population standard deviation of the present values only. Replace each NA with that mean, then convert every value to a z-score: (value - mean) / std. If std is 0, every z-score is 0. If no values are present, print only the line no data.

revision: Python is the glue; NumPy, PyTorch and similar libraries do the heavy maths in compiled code.

days.title: Linear Algebra Essentials: Vectors, Matrices and the Dot Product
days.focus: Linear algebra is the mathematics of vectors (ordered lists of numbers) and matrices (rectangular grids of numbers) and the linear operations on them. In AI, a data point is a vector of features, a dataset is a matrix, a neural-network layer is a matrix multiplication followed by a non-linearity, and an embedding is a vector whose direction encodes meaning.
objectives: Represent data, model weights and embeddings as vectors and matrices.
Compute and interpret dot products, norms and cosine similarity.
Apply the shape rule for matrix multiplication and spot shape errors quickly.
Explain transpose, identity, inverse, rank and eigenvectors at an interview level.
Implement matrix multiplication by hand with a shape check.
days.assignment: Read matrix A (m x n) and matrix B (n2 x p) of integers. If n is not equal to n2, print shape mismatch: (m,n) @ (n2,p). Otherwise compute C = A @ B, print its shape, its rows, and its trace (sum of the main diagonal) if C is square, or trace=n/a if it is not.
steps: Read the concept and work through the example
Implement the practice task without opening the solution
Run the provided cases and add an edge case
Explain your result and complete the revision checklist
revision: Data, weights and embeddings are vectors and matrices; check shapes first when debugging.
(m, n) @ (n, p) gives (m, p); inner dimensions must match.
Dot product measures alignment; cosine similarity compares direction only.
Matrix multiplication is not commutative and is different from element-wise multiplication.
Rank counts independent directions; low-rank ideas power PCA, SVD and LoRA.
A layer's compute cost is roughly m * n * p multiply-adds.

days.title: Probability and Statistics for Machine Learning
days.focus: Probability is the mathematics of uncertainty: it assigns numbers between 0 and 1 to events and describes how likely different outcomes are. Statistics uses data to estimate those probabilities and the parameters of distributions. Machine learning models are statistical models: a classifier outputs a probability distribution over classes and training chooses the parameters that make the observed data most likely.
objectives: Explain random variables, distributions, expectation and variance in plain terms.
Apply conditional probability and Bayes' theorem to realistic problems.
Recognise the normal, Bernoulli, binomial and categorical distributions in ML.
Connect maximum likelihood to common loss functions such as MSE and cross-entropy.
Avoid base-rate mistakes when interpreting classifier outputs.
days.assignment: Read the prior probability of the condition, the test sensitivity P(+ | condition) and the specificity P(- | no condition). Compute P(+), the posterior P(condition | +) and P(condition | -). If the conditioning event has probability 0 (smaller than 1e-12), print undefined for that posterior.
steps: Read the concept and work through the example
Implement the practice task without opening the solution
Run the provided cases and add an edge case
Explain your result and complete the revision checklist
revision: Classifier outputs are probability distributions: Bernoulli for binary, categorical for multi-class.
Bayes' theorem combines a prior with evidence; ignoring the prior causes base-rate errors.
Use median and percentiles for skewed data such as latency.
Minimising MSE or cross-entropy is maximum likelihood under Gaussian or Bernoulli assumptions.
L2 regularisation is equivalent to a Gaussian prior on the weights.
A p-value is not the probability that your model is better.

days.title: The Machine Learning Workflow: From Problem Framing to Baselines
days.focus: The machine learning workflow is the repeatable sequence of steps used to turn a business problem into a working model: frame the problem, collect and understand data, prepare features, split the data, establish a baseline, train and tune models, evaluate on held-out data, deploy and monitor. Each step has typical failure modes, and most real-world ML failures come from data and process mistakes rather than from the choice of algorithm.
objectives: Describe the end-to-end ML lifecycle from problem framing to monitoring.
Frame a business problem as an ML task with a measurable target and metric.
Split data into train, validation and test sets correctly, including time-based splits.
Identify and prevent data leakage.
Build a simple baseline before training complex models.
days.assignment: Labels are given in time order. Hold out the last n_test labels as the test set, where n_test = floor(n * fraction), clamped to the range 1 to n - 1. Using the training labels only, find the majority class (break ties by choosing the alphabetically smallest label). Print the split sizes, the training label counts, the baseline label and the baseline's accuracy on the test set.
steps: Read the concept and work through the example
Implement the practice task without opening the solution
Run the provided cases and add an edge case
Explain your result and complete the revision checklist
revision: Frame the problem first: target, prediction moment, action and metric.
Train fits parameters, validation selects models, test is used once at the end.
Split by time for temporal data and by group for repeated entities.
Leakage gives great offline scores and poor production results; fit preprocessing on train only.
Always compare against a simple baseline such as the majority class.
The workflow is a loop: monitoring in production feeds the next iteration.
